evidence.text: A crescent moon
Pictograph of the moon.
闕也。大陰之精。象形。凡月之屬皆从月。

Pictogram (象形) – pictographic representation of a crescent moon. Related to 夕 (xī) and interchangeable in the past, but both are unrelated to 多, in which it represents two pieces of meat stylized as 夕.
Unrelated to:
* 前, in which it represents a boat 舟 (歬 > 𠝣 > 𣦃 > 前);
* 朕, in which it represents a boat again (𦩎 > 𦨶 > 朕)
* 青, in which it represents cinnabar 丹 (𤯞 > 靑 > 青);
* 赢, in which it represents the elongated face of a kind of dragon, perhaps a Panlong;
* 祭 and 將, in which it represents sacrificed meat stylized as 𱼀;
* 然, in which it represents dog meat (肰).
* 肖 and 有, in which it represents just meat.
From Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-ŋʷ(j)a-t (“moon; star”), whence also Magar [script needed] (gya hot, “moon”), Proto-Lolo-Burmese *mwatᴸ (“star; moon”) (whence Lahu məʔ-kə (“star”)), Drung gurmet (“star”) (Matisoff, 1980; LaPolla, 1987; STEDT).
Various alternative etymologies have also been proposed:
* Unger (1992) proposes cognation with Tibetan ངོ (ngo, “waxing and waning moon; half moon”) (as in མར་ངོ (mar ngo, “waning moon”) and ཡར་ངོ (yar ngo, “waxing moon”)), which Schuessler (2007) connects to Proto-Sino-Tibetan *s-ŋow (“white; light colour”). However, Sagart (1999) points out that the Tibetan word may be analyzed as a derivative of Tibetan ངོ (ngo, “face”), which would mean the semantic connection between “moon” and “face” had to occur either independently in Chinese and Tibetan or in Proto-Sino-Tibetan; it also requires positing a suffix -t in Chinese.
* Pulleybank (1995a) proposes another etymology based on the glyph for 名 (míng) (reconstructed as *màŋʲ), which he analyses as a phono-semantic compound of phonetic 夕 (xī, “moon”) and semantic 口 (kǒu, “mouth”). He suggests that the phonetic component represents a lost word *màŋʲ (“moon”), and reconstructs 月 as *mŋʲ (consonantal frame of “moon”) + *-at (suffix) > *ŋʲʷat. However, there are more straightforward ways of explaining the glyph origin of 名 (míng) (see there), which would nullify the hypothesis of the lost word.
* Related to 越 (“to pass over; to cross over”) in some way.
** Mei (1979) derives 月 from 越 (OC **gjot > *gwjat): **N-gjot > *ngwjat. Also in this proposed word family is 歲 (OC **s-gjots > *skwjadh, “year”). The semantics of this word family is centred around "to pass; to elapse". While Matisoff (1980) seems supportive of this word family, STEDT reconstructs Proto-Tibeto-Burman *grwat (“to travel; to go through”) for 越 and 歲 /岁 (suì), separate from the root for 月.
** Ferlus (2012) reconstructs the Old Chinese as *ŋ.wat and puts it in a word family formed from a Chinese root *wat, having a meaning of "circularity" or "circular boundary". This proposed word family includes 越 (OC *wat, “to cross over”), as in "to cross the enclosure of the village", and 外 (OC *ŋ.wat-s, “outside”), as in "out of the enclosure of the village".

evidence.source: Academia Sinica, Institute of History and Philology, Chinese Character Database
evidence.field: 字形演變; basic character explanation
evidence.text: The database shows 月 across oracle-bone, bronze, Chu bamboo/slip, small-seal, and 說文 categories, and describes its form as resembling a crescent moon, with ‘moon’ as its original meaning. This supports a pictographic account; no separate semantic or phonetic component is identified.
evidence.title: 漢字「月」：字形演變

evidence.text: The page lists oracle-bone examples including 甲225 and 甲3941; bronze examples including late Shang and Western Zhou forms; Warring States, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms. Its account says some oracle-bone shapes show the moon’s outline and inner shadow, that bronze forms continue the earlier shapes, and that the form becomes less pictorial through Warring States and clerical development before the regular form stabilizes. This is a secondary synthesis of cited paleographic records, not independent inspection of the glyph images.
evidence.title: 汉字「月」字形演变字源演变

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The entry gives oracle-bone uses for 月 as ‘moon’, including 合集11483正, glossed as ‘之夕，月有食’ (an eclipse of the moon), and as a calendrical month, citing 合集5658正 ‘今十一月帝不其令雨’ and the bronze inscription 曶鼎 ‘唯王元年六月’. It describes the month sense as arising from the moon’s waxing-and-waning cycle. These are source-reported readings and glosses; they do not establish that ‘month’ was later than ‘moon’ solely by list order.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database; citing 裘錫圭
evidence.field: oracle-bone component analysis; 月 and 夕 discussion
evidence.text: The entry reports that 月 and 夕 originally shared a moon-shaped graph and that presence or absence of an interior dot was initially not distinguishing; later graphic specialization assigned the dotted form to 月 and the undotted form to 夕. It separately says 月 is a half-moon pictograph and traces the calendar-month use to the lunar cycle. This is a reported paleographic analysis, not evidence that 月 is a phonetic component in 夕 or vice versa.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

evidence.source: Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.text: The dictionary lists distinct senses: moon, moonlight, monthly/each month, round forms resembling the moon, a time-counting classifier/unit, surname, and radical. It cites classical examples for several senses, including 《詩經》「七月流火」 and 《書經·洪範》「一曰歲，二曰月」. This supports a range of later documented uses but the page does not date the first occurrence of each semantic extension.
evidence.title: [A01841] 月 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Xu Shen, Shuowen Jiezi, as quoted in Taiwan Ministry of Education, Dictionary of Chinese Character Variants
evidence.field: 釋義; 說文解字(大徐本)
evidence.text: The entry quotes the Shuowen definition ‘月，闕也。太陰之精。’ and lists the Shuowen witness at 月部, 卷七上, 頁4右. Shuowen classifies the form as 象形 in the dossier quotation; this is a historical lexicographic account and is consistent with the independently reported ancient shapes, but the later oracle-bone evidence is earlier than Shuowen.
evidence.title: [A01841] 月 - 教育部《異體字字典》

evidence.source: Tang Tao and Deng Fei, Journal of Chinese Writing Systems
evidence.text: The 2020 study concerns the relatively fixed and also variable writing positions of numeral-month graphs in Shang oracle-bone inscriptions. Its abstract attributes special positions to inscription layout, divination cracks, line direction, the nature of numeral-month notation, and writing material. It supports the calendrical context of Shang month notation, but does not resolve the character’s word etymology.
evidence.title: Analysis of the causes of the formation of the special writing position of the month in oracle bone inscriptions

evidence.source: Chinese University of Hong Kong, Multi-function Chinese Character Database
evidence.text: The database presents 名 as composed of 夕 and 口 and explains it through speaking one’s name in darkness; it does not support the dossier’s alternative that 夕 is a phonetic representing a lost word for ‘moon’ in 名. Because the proposed moon-word reconstruction and phonetic interpretation were not verified in an accessible primary source during this search, the Pulleyblank proposal remains unsubstantiated here; a shared/related graph is not itself evidence for a sound component.
evidence.title: 漢語多功能字庫：漢字甲骨部件分析

editorial_rules: Write about the character's graphic history; distinguish it from the history of a spoken word.
Separate historical explanation from mnemonics. Do not infer history from modern shapes or readings.
Sources may repeat one another. A source count is not independent corroboration.
Treat Shuowen as a historical account, not automatic confirmation. Its generated English glosses are excluded.
Unrelated word senses may appear in Wiktionary excerpts. Do not merge them into a character origin.
Related-character evidence retains its record_character. Do not silently transfer a traditional form's components to a simplified form.
No glyph image has been visually inspected in this packet. Do not claim to have inspected one.
Explain missing evidence explicitly, especially for Japanese-created characters. A Chinese spelling pronunciation is not evidence for a Japanese origin.

items.period: Shang oracle-bone script; source record is identified as 簠天1, 合33694, 歷組
items.caption: This oracle-script form has a long central stroke and a curved outer stroke that frame a crescent-shaped opening, a shape consistent with 月 as a moon pictograph.
items.alt: Black glyph with a long vertical stroke beside a curved outer stroke, leaving a crescent-shaped opening.
items.selection_reason: The visible strokes match the documented half-moon pictographic account. The form is identified with a specific Shang oracle-bone record.
items.rights: CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication, as stated on the Commons page for the Sinica-derived image.

items.period: Shuowen small-seal script tradition; the image is a modern vector reconstruction
items.caption: This small-seal form has a rounded enclosing outline, an interior cross-stroke, and a curved extension below.
items.alt: Black rounded glyph with an oval outline, a short interior stroke, a cross-stroke, and a long curved lower extension.
items.selection_reason: It offers a useful graphic comparison: the rounded, less crescent-like outline shows how a later script tradition rendered 月. It is a modern reconstruction of the Shuowen seal-script tradition.
items.rights: Public domain dedication for the SVG representation, as stated on the Commons file page.

limitations.text: Both images are modern redrawings rather than photographs of ancient inscriptions. The oracle form is linked to a specific record, but the precise date of that inscription and the character’s first dated attestation are not established here.
